lesson.title: What to Expect: The Mean of a Binomial Distribution
lesson.summary: The mean of a binomial random variable has a strikingly simple formula, np, that falls directly out of the expected value of a sum of independent trial outcomes.
lesson.body:
For a binomial random variable X with n trials and success probability p, the mean, also called the expected value, has a remarkably clean formula: E(X) = np. Given how much work went into computing individual probabilities in the last two chapters, it might be surprising that the mean requires no combinations and no factorials at all.

The reason traces back to a property of expected value: the expected value of a sum of random variables equals the sum of their individual expected values, whether or not those variables are independent. A binomial random variable X can be thought of as a sum of n separate trial outcomes, where each trial contributes a 1 if it's a success and a 0 if it's a failure. Each individual trial has expected value p, since it equals 1 with probability p and 0 with probability (1 minus p), and 1 x p + 0 x (1 minus p) = p. Adding up n trials, each contributing p to the expectation, gives E(X) = p + p + ... + p (n times) = np.

Check this against the 3 coin flip distribution built earlier: P(X=0)=1/8, P(X=1)=3/8, P(X=2)=3/8, P(X=3)=1/8. Computing the mean directly from the definition, E(X) = 0(1/8) + 1(3/8) + 2(3/8) + 3(1/8) = (0 + 3 + 6 + 3)/8 = 12/8 = 1.5. The formula gives the same answer instantly: np = 3 x 0.5 = 1.5. Both methods agree, which is exactly the kind of cross check worth doing the first time you use a new formula.

Now apply it somewhere the full distribution would be tedious to build by hand. On a 20 question true or false quiz where a student guesses randomly on every question, p = 0.5 and n = 20, so the expected number of correct guesses is np = 20 x 0.5 = 10. That does not mean any particular student guesses exactly 10 right, it means that if many students each guessed randomly on all 20 questions, the average number correct across all of them would land close to 10.
